Euclid, the Elements, and twenty-one problems from the most successful math book ever written

A bald teacher bends almost double over a slate on the floor, a compass in his hand, while his students crowd in: one kneels close enough to touch it, one points, one turns to explain it to a friend. For centuries this figure has been called Euclid (some say Archimedes). Chapter One · Alexandria · about 300 BC

The Man Nobody Knows

In 331 BC, Alexander the Great marched into Egypt and marked out a new city on the Mediterranean coast. He named it after himself: Alexandria. Eight years later Alexander was dead, and one of his generals, Ptolemy, took Egypt for himself and made Alexandria his capital. Ptolemy wanted a capital of ideas, not just of soldiers. He (or his son, who ruled after him) built the Museum, a "home of the Muses" where scholars were paid to study and teach, and beside it the Library, which tried to collect a copy of every book in the world.

Somewhere in that city, around 300 BC, a teacher named Euclid wrote a book called the Elements. It became probably the most successful textbook in history. It was copied by hand for 1,800 years, printed over and over after that, and used in classrooms until about a hundred years ago.

The strange part is how little we know about the man. No portrait. No birthplace. No date of birth or death. Our main source is a philosopher named Proclus, who wrote about Euclid around AD 450, roughly 750 years later. Even Proclus only knew that Euclid lived while the first Ptolemy was king: after Plato's students, and before Archimedes.

Two stories about him survive, and you should treat both with care. The story goes that King Ptolemy asked Euclid whether there was a shorter way to learn geometry than working through the whole Elements. Euclid answered: "There is no royal road to geometry." Proclus tells this story, but the very same line is also told about a different mathematician, Menaechmus, talking to Alexander. A good line tends to get passed around. The second story comes from a writer named Stobaeus, even later, around AD 500. A student who had just learned his first proposition asked, "What will I get from learning this?" Euclid called his servant and said, "Give him a coin, since he must make a profit from what he learns."

What we do have is the book. The Elements has 13 books (we would call them chapters) and 465 propositions: things to be built, and things to be proved. It does not start with a problem. It starts with definitions, so that everyone agrees on the words. Definition 1: "A point is that which has no part." Definition 2: "A line is breadthless length."

Next come five postulates, things you are allowed to do or assume without proof. You may draw a straight line from any point to any point. You may extend a straight line as far as you like. You may draw a circle with any centre and any radius. All right angles are equal. The fifth postulate is long and odd, and it will cause trouble for two thousand years; we will meet it properly at the end. Last come five common notions, such as "things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another" and "the whole is greater than the part."

After that, nothing is allowed in unless it is proved, using only the definitions, the postulates, the common notions and the propositions already proved before it. Much of the mathematics was not new. An earlier mathematician, Hippocrates of Chios, had written an Elements more than a century before (it is lost), and Euclid used the work of Eudoxus and Theaetetus, who had worked with Plato. Euclid's genius was the order: a single chain of reasoning where every link holds. It was so good that the older books stopped being copied, and vanished.

Here is how the book defines a circle (Definitions 15 and 16): a round figure with a point inside, the centre, such that all the straight lines from the centre out to the edge are equal. We call each of those lines a radius. Definition 17: a diameter is a straight line through the centre that ends at the circle on both sides.

🌟 Big Idea #1: In the Elements, "it looks true" is never enough. Every claim must be proved from what came before, so anyone can check it, step by step, without having to trust the author.
★ Checkpoint 1 · Book I, Definitions 15 to 17
A circle has a radius of 7 cm. How long is its diameter?
cm
A diameter runs from the edge, through the centre, to the far edge: one radius in, one radius out.
Chapter Two · Book I, Proposition 1

Two Circles and a Triangle

Proposition 1 is the very first thing Euclid does with his rules: "On a given finite straight line, to construct an equilateral triangle." In plain words: you are handed a line. Build a triangle on it with all three sides equal.

Notice the tools. No ruler with numbers on it. No protractor. Postulates 1 to 3 allow exactly two tools: a straightedge, which only draws straight lines, and a compass, which only draws circles. Euclid never measures anything. He proves.

Book I, Proposition 1 · straightedge and compass
Step 0 of 4

Euclid's argument for why the sides are equal uses only two facts from the start of the book. The first is Definition 15: all the radii of one circle are equal. The second is Common Notion 1: things equal to the same thing are equal to each other. Look at the finished picture and see if you can put them together before you answer.

At the end of a construction Euclid writes, in Greek, "which is what it was required to do." Later Latin translators shortened this to Q.E.F. At the end of a proved theorem he writes "which is what it was required to prove," in Latin quod erat demonstrandum: Q.E.D. Mathematicians still write Q.E.D. at the end of proofs today.

🔎 An honest note. Euclid never proves that the two circles actually cross. It looks obvious in the picture. By his own rules, though, a picture is not a proof, and nothing in his postulates says that two circles must meet. Readers spotted gaps like this over the centuries. In 1899 the German mathematician David Hilbert wrote out a fuller set of starting rules for geometry that fills them. The chain was stronger than anyone had a right to expect, but it was not perfect.

Chapter Three · Book I, Propositions 13 and 15

Where Two Lines Cross

Euclid never uses degrees. He measures angles in right angles, the square corner. Proposition 13 says: when one straight line stands on another, the two angles it makes beside each other add up to two right angles. In degrees, where a right angle is 90°, that is 180°. A straight line is a half-turn.

Proposition 15 is about two straight lines that cross, like an X. They make four angles. The angles opposite each other (across the crossing point, not side by side) are always equal. Proclus says this fact was first discovered by Thales, a Greek thinker who lived around 600 BC, about three hundred years before Euclid. It was Euclid who gave it a proof.

The proof is short. Call the four angles, going round, p, q, r and s. Angles p and q sit side by side on one straight line, so by Proposition 13, p + q = 180°. Angles q and r sit side by side on the other straight line, so q + r = 180°. Now subtract q from both:

p + q = 180°  so  p = 180° − q
q + r = 180°  so  r = 180° − q
Both equal 180° − q, so p = r. (Common Notions 1 and 3.)

Turn the slanted line and watch the numbers.

Two crossing lines · turn one of them

Chapter Four · Book I, Propositions 5 and 32

The Bridge of Asses

A triangle with two equal sides is called isosceles (eye-SOSS-uh-leez), Greek for "equal legs." Proposition 5 says that in an isosceles triangle, the two angles at the base (the angles where the equal sides meet the third side) are equal. Proclus says Thales knew this too.

Euclid's proof is famous for being tricky: he extends the two equal sides downward and compares two pairs of overlapping triangles. Generations of students got stuck right there. In the Middle Ages it earned a nickname: pons asinorum, Latin for "the bridge of asses." An ass is a donkey. If you could not get over this bridge, you were the donkey. (Euclid's drawing, with its extended sides, even looks a little like a bridge.)

Proposition 32 is one of the most useful facts in all of geometry: the three angles of any triangle add up to two right angles, 180°. Here is Euclid's idea. Through the top corner, draw a line parallel to the base. The parallel line makes an angle equal to a on the left and an angle equal to b on the right (that is Proposition 29). Now look at the top corner: a, c and b sit side by side along a straight line. By Proposition 13, they make 180°.

The same proposition gives a bonus. Extend one side of a triangle past a corner. The angle outside, the exterior angle, equals the two inside angles at the other two corners added together. Here is why, with the inside angles called a, b and c, and the exterior angle beside c called e:

e + c = 180°  (side by side on a straight line, Prop 13)
a + b + c = 180°  (the three angles of the triangle)
Both make 180°, so take c away from each: e = a + b.
⚠️ Remember the odd fifth postulate from Chapter One? Proposition 29, the one about parallel lines, is the first place in the whole book where Euclid needs it. Every triangle in the world adding up to 180° depends on that postulate. Keep it in mind. It comes back at the end.
★ Checkpoint 6 · Book I, Propositions 5 and 32
An isosceles triangle has an angle of 40° at the top, between its two equal sides. How big is each of the two base angles?
degrees
All three angles make 180°. Take away the 40° at the top, then share what is left equally between the two base angles (Proposition 5 says they are equal).
★ Checkpoint 7 · Book I, Proposition 32
A triangle has angles of 50° and 60° at its two bottom corners. One side is extended past the top corner. How big is the exterior angle there?
degrees
The exterior angle equals the two inside angles at the other two corners, added together.
Chapter Five · Book I, Proposition 20

What Every Donkey Knows

Proposition 20: in any triangle, any two sides added together are longer than the third side. Put another way, a straight path is shorter than any path with a bend in it.

Some ancient Greeks thought proving this was silly. Proclus reports that followers of the philosopher Epicurus made fun of it: even a donkey knows it. Put the donkey at one corner of a triangle and the hay at another, and the donkey walks straight to the hay. It does not wander off to the third corner first.

Proclus answered the joke. Knowing that something is true is not the same as knowing why it is true. The donkey can walk the short way, but it cannot explain it. There is a second, deeper reason. If Euclid let in one "obvious" fact without proof, which others would he let in? Some things that look obvious turn out to be false. The only safe rule is the hard one: prove everything.

The proposition is also practical. Proposition 22 shows how to build a triangle out of any three lengths, as long as each pair of them, added together, is longer than the third. If they are not, the two short sides cannot reach each other, or they lie flat along the long one.

Two pages of Vatican manuscript Greek 190, written out by hand in the 800s or 900s AD. Find the diagram for Proposition 47 in the middle of the right-hand page: a triangle with a square on each side. This copy is special. Nearly every other Greek manuscript of the Elements comes from Theon's edition of the 300s AD. In the early 1800s, when Napoleon's armies had carried the manuscript off to Paris, a French scholar named François Peyrard noticed that this one does not. It is our best window onto Euclid's text before Theon's changes. Look in the margins too: readers over the centuries squeezed in their own notes.

Chapter Six · Book I, Propositions 47 and 48

The End of Book One

All of Book I builds toward its last two propositions. Proposition 47: in a right-angled triangle, the square on the side opposite the right angle equals the squares on the other two sides. The two sides that make the square corner are the legs, and the long side across from it is the hypotenuse. With legs a and b and hypotenuse c:

📐 Book I, Proposition 47: a² + b² = c². (a², "a squared," means a × a: the area of a square with side a.)

It carries the name of Pythagoras, who lived more than two hundred years before Euclid, though people in Babylon were using the rule more than a thousand years before Pythagoras. The proof in the Elements is a clever one. It cuts the big square into two rectangles and shows that each one matches one of the smaller squares. Proclus believed that this particular proof was Euclid's own.

Try the most famous example. With legs 3 and 4: 3 × 3 = 9 and 4 × 4 = 16, and 9 + 16 = 25. Since 5 × 5 = 25, the hypotenuse is 5. Nobody had to measure the long side. It was calculated.

Proposition 48 runs the other way: if the squares on two sides add up to the square on the third, then the angle between those two sides is a right angle. A carpenter can check whether a corner is truly square by measuring 3 along one edge, 4 along the other, and checking that the diagonal is exactly 5.

★ Checkpoint 9 · Book I, Proposition 47

units
8 × 8 = 64 and 15 × 15 = 225. Add them, then ask: what number times itself makes that? Try numbers just above 15.
P.Oxy. I 29, a scrap of papyrus pulled from the ancient rubbish heaps of Oxyrhynchus in Egypt by Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt, and published in 1898. The Greek words are the statement of Book II, Proposition 5, and the little drawing at the lower right is its diagram: a long rectangle with a square beside it, cut by lines. The red 29 is a modern catalogue number. Experts still argue over its age, with dates from about AD 75 to about AD 300. Either way, someone was studying Euclid in a small Egyptian town and threw the page away. It is now in the Penn Museum in Philadelphia (E2748).

Chapter Seven · Book II, Proposition 4

Algebra Made of Squares

The Greeks had no algebra symbols: no x, no little raised 2, no equals sign. They did their algebra with shapes. Book II of the Elements is full of it.

Proposition 4 says: cut a straight line anywhere into two pieces. The square on the whole line equals the squares on the two pieces, plus twice the rectangle made from the two pieces. That sounds like a mouthful until you see it:

The whole square has side a + b. Inside it sit a square on a, a square on b, and two rectangles that are each a by b. In today's symbols:

(a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²

You can use it to square numbers in your head. Take 12 × 12. Split 12 into 10 + 2. The big square is 10 × 10 = 100, the small one 2 × 2 = 4, and the two rectangles are 10 × 2 = 20 each, so 40. Add them: 100 + 40 + 4 = 144.

In the 1890s two young scholars from Oxford, Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt, dug through the ancient rubbish heaps of an Egyptian town called Oxyrhynchus, where the dry sand had preserved thousands of scraps of papyrus. One scrap, catalogued as P.Oxy. I 29, has the words of the very next proposition, Book II, Proposition 5, along with its diagram of a rectangle and a square. Experts disagree about its age; guesses run from about AD 75 to about AD 300. It is one of the oldest pieces of the Elements that survive, and it is now in the Penn Museum in Philadelphia.

★ Checkpoint 10 · Book II, Proposition 4
A square has side 7, cut into 3 + 4. Proposition 4 says
7² = 3² + (the two rectangles) + 4².
What is the area of the two rectangles together? Work it out both ways if you can.
square units
One way: each rectangle is 3 by 4. Another way: 7² = 49, 3² = 9 and 4² = 16, so 49 = 9 + (rectangles) + 16. What is 49 − 9 − 16?
Chapter Eight · Book III, Proposition 31

The Corner in the Semicircle

Book III is about circles. Proposition 31 holds a surprise. Draw a circle and a diameter across it. Pick any point on the curve and join it to both ends of the diameter. The angle at that point is always a right angle. Move the point anywhere you like along the half circle. It stays 90°.

Book III, Proposition 31 · slide the corner round the circle

Why? Draw the dashed line from the centre O out to the corner. It is a radius, and so are OA and OB. That splits the big triangle into two isosceles triangles. By Proposition 5, each one has two equal base angles: call them a and a on the left, b and b on the right. The angle at the corner on the circle is a + b. Now add up all the angles of the big triangle:

a + a + b + b = 180°  (Proposition 32)
2a + 2b = 180°
a + b = 90°  (halve both sides)

The story goes that Thales discovered this and was so delighted that he sacrificed an ox to the gods. That story comes from a writer named Diogenes Laertius, around AD 200 to 250, about 800 years after Thales lived. Even Diogenes admits that other writers gave the discovery, and the ox, to Pythagoras instead.

★ Checkpoint 11 · Book III, Proposition 31
A triangle is drawn in a semicircle with the diameter as its longest side. The angle at one end of the diameter is 35°. How big is the angle at the other end?
degrees
The corner on the circle is 90°. The three angles make 180°: 180 − 90 − 35.
Chapter Nine · Book IV, Proposition 15

Six Triangles in a Circle

Book IV fits regular shapes (all sides equal, all angles equal) inside circles. Proposition 15 does it for the hexagon, the six-sided shape of a honeycomb cell. At the end of it Euclid adds a short note: the side of the hexagon is equal to the radius of the circle.

That means you can draw one with just a compass. Open the compass to the radius, put the point anywhere on the circle, and mark where it lands on the curve. Move the point to that mark and step again. After exactly six steps you are back where you started.

Here is why it works, using propositions you already know. Join the centre to all six corners. That makes six triangles that meet at the centre, sharing the full turn of 360°, so each one has 60° at the centre (360 ÷ 6). Two sides of each triangle are radii, so each triangle is isosceles, and its two base angles are equal (Proposition 5). Together they make 180° − 60° = 120°, so each base angle is 60°. All three angles are 60°. A triangle with equal angles has equal sides (Proposition 6), so the outer side of each triangle, the side of the hexagon, is as long as a radius.

★ Checkpoint 12 · Book IV, Proposition 15
A regular hexagon is drawn inside a circle of radius 5 cm, its corners touching the circle. What is the hexagon's perimeter (all six sides together)?
cm
Each side equals the radius. There are six sides.
Chapter Ten · Book VII, Propositions 1 and 2

The Oldest Algorithm

Books VII, VIII and IX are about whole numbers, though Euclid still pictures every number as a length. Proposition 2 asks: given two numbers, find the biggest number that measures both of them exactly (divides into both with nothing left over). We call it the greatest common divisor. Euclid calls it the greatest common measure.

His method is beautifully simple. Take the smaller number away from the larger. Then do it again with the two numbers you now have. Keep going. When the two numbers are equal, that number is the answer.

Try 20 and 8. 20 − 8 = 12. Now 12 and 8: 12 − 8 = 4. Now 8 and 4: 8 − 4 = 4. Now 4 and 4: equal. So the greatest common measure of 20 and 8 is 4. Check: 4 goes into 20 five times and into 8 twice.

You can see it as a picture. Make a rectangle 20 by 8. Cut off the biggest square you can, then the biggest square from what is left, and so on. The last square fits exactly into both sides. Try it:

Euclid’s algorithm · cut off the biggest square you can

Proposition 1 covers the other ending: if the subtracting only stops when you reach 1, then nothing bigger than 1 measures both numbers. Euclid calls such numbers "prime to one another." (Try 13 × 8 above.)

A step-by-step recipe like this, one that always finishes with the right answer, is called an algorithm, and this is one of the oldest still in use. Computers use versions of it to simplify fractions. The encryption that keeps online shopping safe uses it too. The computer scientist Donald Knuth called it "the granddaddy of all algorithms."

★ Checkpoint 13 · Book VII, Proposition 2
Use Euclid's method to find the greatest common measure of 84 and 36.
84 − 36 = 48. Then 48 − 36 = 12. Now you have 36 and 12. Keep taking the smaller from the larger until the two numbers match.
★ Checkpoint 14 · Book VII, Proposition 2
Now 91 and 35. What is their greatest common measure?
91 − 35 = 56, then 56 − 35 = 21, then 35 − 21 = 14. Keep going.
Chapter Eleven · Book IX, Proposition 20

The Primes Never Run Out

A prime number is a number that only 1 and itself can measure: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23... Every other whole number above 1 can be built by multiplying primes together, like 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. Primes are the atoms of arithmetic.

As you count higher, primes get rarer. Between 1 and 100 there are 25 of them. Between 9,900 and 10,000 there are only 9. Do they eventually stop? Is there a biggest prime?

Proposition 20 of Book IX answers, in Euclid's careful words: "Prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers." Notice that he never says infinite. Greek mathematicians were wary of the infinite. Instead Euclid says: give me any list of primes you like, and I can show you a prime that is not on it.

Here is how. Multiply every prime on the list together, then add 1. Call the result N. Now try dividing N by any prime on your list. It always leaves a remainder of 1, because N is one more than a multiple of that prime. That means no prime on your list measures N. Then one of two things is true:

① N is prime itself. It is a new prime, not on your list.
② N is not prime. Then some prime measures it, and that prime cannot be on your list. Again, a new prime.

Either way, your list was missing a prime. No list can ever hold them all. Euclid's own proof uses a list of just three primes, but the argument works for any list at all. For example, with the list 2, 3, 5: 2 × 3 × 5 + 1 = 31, and 31 is a prime not on the list.

★ Checkpoint 15 · Book IX, Proposition 20
Take the list of primes 2, 3, 5, 7. Follow Euclid's recipe: multiply them all together, then add 1. What number do you get? (It happens to be prime.)
2 × 3 = 6, 6 × 5 = 30, 30 × 7 = 210. Then add 1.
★ Checkpoint 16 · Book IX, Proposition 20 · testing the proof
Now take the list 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13. Multiply and add 1: you get 30,031. But 30,031 = 59 × 509, so it is not prime! Does that break Euclid's proof?
Chapter Twelve · Book IX, Proposition 36

Perfect Numbers

Book VII defines a perfect number: a number equal to the sum of its own parts, meaning all the numbers smaller than itself that measure it exactly. The smallest is 6. Its parts are 1, 2 and 3, and 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

The next one is 28. Its parts are 1, 2, 4, 7 and 14 (try dividing 28 by each), and 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 = 28. After that they get rare very fast.

The last proposition of Book IX, Proposition 36, is a recipe for making them. Start at 1 and keep doubling: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... Add them up as you go. Whenever the running total is a prime, multiply that total by the last number you added. The answer is a perfect number.

1 + 2 = 3, which is prime: 3 × 2 = 6
1 + 2 + 4 = 7, which is prime: 7 × 4 = 28
1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15, which is not prime (3 × 5), so skip it
and carry on doubling...

About two thousand years later, in the 1700s, the Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler proved that it works the other way round too: every even perfect number comes from Euclid's recipe. What about odd perfect numbers? Nobody has ever found one. Nobody has ever proved that none exist. It is one of the oldest unsolved problems in mathematics, and it is still open today. Maybe you will be the one to settle it.

★ Checkpoint 17 · Book IX, Proposition 36
Keep doubling: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16. Add them up and check that the total is prime. Then follow Euclid's recipe: multiply the total by the last number you added. Which perfect number do you get?
1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31, which is prime. Now 31 × 16: that is 31 × 10 plus 31 × 6.
Chapter Thirteen · Book XIII, Propositions 13 to 18

Only Five

The last book of the Elements climbs to the top of the mountain. A regular solid is a 3D shape whose faces are all the same regular polygon, with the same number meeting at every corner. Book XIII builds all five: the tetrahedron (4 triangles), the octahedron (8 triangles), the icosahedron (20 triangles), the cube (6 squares) and the dodecahedron (12 pentagons). Plato wrote about these five shapes, which is why they are often called the Platonic solids. Much of the work on them goes back to Plato's friend Theaetetus.

After Proposition 18, Euclid adds a remarkable claim: there are no others. Not "nobody has found another one yet." There cannot be another one, ever. Here is the reason, from Book XI, Proposition 21. At every corner of a solid, at least three faces must meet, and the flat angles that meet there must add up to less than 360°. If they add up to exactly 360°, the faces lie flat. With more than 360°, they will not fit at all.

Try it with the triangles and squares. Each corner of an equilateral triangle is 60°, and each corner of a square is 90°.

Build a corner · can it fold up into a solid?
Pentagons and hexagons are yours to work out in the checkpoints below.

Now the bigger shapes. Each corner of a regular pentagon is 108°, and each corner of a regular hexagon is 120°.

★ Checkpoint 18 · Book XIII, after Proposition 18
Three regular pentagons meet at one corner. Each corner of a pentagon is 108°. What do the three angles add up to?
degrees
3 × 108 = 3 × 100 + 3 × 8.
★ Checkpoint 19 · Book XIII, after Proposition 18 · the proof
324° is less than 360°, so three pentagons can make a corner: that is the dodecahedron. Why can there be no regular solid made of hexagons?

Chapter Fourteen · Book VI, Proposition 4

Six Books by Candlelight

Euclid's own copy of the Elements is long gone. The book survived because people kept copying it by hand, one scribe after another, for more than 1,700 years. In the 300s AD, Theon of Alexandria (the father of the mathematician Hypatia) made his own edition, adding small changes and fixes. Nearly every Greek copy that survives comes from Theon's version.

Around AD 800, in Baghdad, a scholar named al-Hajjaj translated the Elements into Arabic. Later in the same century Ishaq ibn Hunayn made a new translation, and the great mathematician Thabit ibn Qurra revised it. For centuries, mathematicians writing in Arabic studied the book, commented on it, and argued about it. In the 1120s, an Englishman named Adelard of Bath, who had travelled widely and learned Arabic, put it into Latin, the language of Europe's scholars.

In 1482, in Venice, a printer named Erhard Ratdolt produced the first printed Elements, with its diagrams printed in the margins. Hundreds of editions followed. In 1847, an Irish teacher named Oliver Byrne printed one where the diagrams and even the proofs were in red, yellow, blue and black instead of letters, "for the greater ease of learners," as his title page says.

One of the book's most famous students was a self-taught lawyer from Illinois. In a short life story he wrote in 1860 (in the third person, for a campaign biography), Abraham Lincoln said that after serving in Congress he "studied and nearly mastered the six books of Euclid." His law partner William Herndon remembered, many years later, Lincoln studying geometry late at night by candlelight while travelling from court to court.

"The six books" were the usual school course: Books I to VI, plane geometry. Book VI, the last of them, is about similar figures, shapes with the same angles but different sizes. Proposition 4 says that if two triangles have the same angles, their sides are in the same proportion. If one side of the big triangle is 3 times its partner in the small triangle, every side is 3 times its partner.

That lets you measure things you cannot reach. At the same moment, the sun's rays strike a stick and a tall tower at the same slant. Each one and its shadow make a right triangle, and the two triangles have the same angles. The story goes that Thales measured the height of an Egyptian pyramid this way, but that story was written down centuries after him. The geometry, though, is pure Book VI.

★ Checkpoint 20 · Book VI, Proposition 4
A stick 2 m tall casts a shadow 3 m long. At the same moment, an obelisk casts a shadow 45 m long. The two triangles have the same angles. How tall is the obelisk?
metres
The obelisk's shadow is 45 ÷ 3 = 15 times as long as the stick's shadow. By Proposition 4, its height is 15 times the stick's height too. Or: height ÷ 45 = 2 ÷ 3.
A page of Book I from an Arabic version of the Elements, printed in Rome in 1594 under the name of the Persian astronomer and mathematician Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, who lived in the 1200s (some historians think this version was written by one of his followers). The diagrams are labelled with Arabic letters instead of Greek ones, and the text runs from right to left. Al-Tusi was one of the many scholars who tried to prove the fifth postulate, and European mathematicians who took up the same puzzle in the 1600s and 1700s read the arguments in this printed book (Harvard, Houghton Library).
An Arabic Elements, printed in Rome, 1594 · hover to unroll · click to enlarge
Chapter Fifteen · Book I, Postulate 5 and Proposition 29

The Postulate That Would Not Behave

Here, at last, is the fifth postulate, in plain words. Draw a straight line crossing two other straight lines. Look at the two inside angles on one side of it. If they add up to less than two right angles (less than 180°), then the two lines, if you extend them far enough, will meet on that side.

Compare that with the other four postulates, which are short and simple. This one reads more like a theorem, something that ought to be proved. Euclid himself seems to have avoided it as long as he could: he proves 28 propositions without it, and uses it for the first time in Proposition 29, to show what happens when a line crosses two parallel lines (lines that never meet). The alternate angles are equal, and the two inside angles on the same side add up to exactly two right angles, 180°.

For about two thousand years, mathematicians tried to prove the fifth postulate from the other four, so that it could be removed from the list. Proclus tried. In Persia, the poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam tried, and so did Nasir al-Din al-Tusi. In Italy in 1733, a priest named Giovanni Saccheri wrote a whole book claiming to have done it. Every attempt failed. Each "proof" quietly assumed something that turned out to be the fifth postulate in disguise.

Then, in the 1820s and 1830s, two young men tried something braver. In Russia, Nikolai Lobachevsky, and in Hungary, János Bolyai, each asked: what if the fifth postulate is simply false? What if, through a point next to a line, you could draw many lines that never meet it? They expected to run into a contradiction. They never did. Instead they found a whole new geometry, just as solid as Euclid's, in which the angles of a triangle add up to less than 180°. (The great German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss had reached similar ideas privately, and never published them.)

János's father, Farkas Bolyai, had spent years on the parallel problem himself. He wrote to his son begging him to leave it alone, warning that it could swallow up his whole life and all his happiness, as it had nearly done to him. János kept going anyway, and in 1832 his work was printed as an appendix to his father's book.

The fifth postulate, it turned out, cannot be proved. It is a genuine choice. Choose it, and you get Euclid's flat geometry. Choose something else, and you get curved geometries that are just as logical. In 1915, Albert Einstein used curved geometry to describe gravity: near heavy objects like the Sun, space itself does not follow Euclid's rules exactly. Euclid's chain of reasoning was so careful that, 2,000 years later, it showed exactly which link could be changed.

★ Checkpoint 21 · Book I, Proposition 29
A straight line crosses two parallel lines. Between the parallels, on the right of the crossing line, the lower angle is 65°. How big is the upper angle on that same side, marked ?
degrees
Proposition 29: for parallel lines, the two inside angles on the same side add up to exactly 180°.
Epilogue

✦ The Chain Still Holds ✦

Look back at what you have done. You started with a point, that which has no part, and a few rules about straight lines and circles. From those alone you built an equilateral triangle, proved that crossing lines make equal angles, found that every triangle holds exactly 180°, squared a sum with pictures, ran the oldest algorithm in the world, chased the primes forever, and showed why there can only ever be five perfect solids. Every step leaned on the steps before it, and every step can be checked by anyone, anywhere, without trusting anybody.

That way of working is Euclid's real gift, bigger than any single theorem. When Isaac Newton wrote his great book on gravity in 1687, he laid it out like the Elements: definitions first, then laws, then propositions, each one proved. Scientists, lawyers and computer programmers still argue the same way: say exactly what you are assuming, and then show that everything else follows.

The fifth postulate taught a second lesson. For two thousand years people tried to prove it and failed. When Lobachevsky and Bolyai finally asked what if it is false?, they did not find nonsense. They found new worlds. A starting assumption is a choice, and it is worth knowing which ones you have made.

Nobody knows what Euclid looked like, where he was born, or when he died. We have his book. After 2,300 years it is still being read, and every proof in it still works. There is no royal road. There never was. You walked the ordinary road, one step at a time, and you got there.

The Society of the Straightedge and Compass
certifies that
Astronomer
has completed all 21 checkpoints of the tale of Euclid's Elements
and is hereby granted the rank of
⭐ Keeper of the Elements ⭐

What you now know that most adults don't:

① The Elements starts from definitions, five postulates and five common notions, and proves 465 propositions from them, each using only what came before.

② Angles side by side on a straight line make 180°; crossing lines make equal opposite angles; every triangle's angles add up to 180°; any two sides of a triangle are longer than the third.

③ Euclid did algebra with shapes: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² is Book II, Proposition 4.

④ Euclid's algorithm finds the greatest common measure of two numbers by subtracting, and computers still use it. There is no biggest prime. There are only five regular solids.

⑤ The fifth postulate cannot be proved from the others. Change it, and you get a different geometry, one that Einstein needed to describe gravity.

⑥ When you read the story goes, ask who wrote it down, and how long afterwards.
